concept.name: Market risk
concept.definition: The risk of losses in on- and off-balance-sheet positions arising from movements in market prices — interest rates, equities, foreign exchange, commodities, credit spreads, and volatilities. It is the risk class for which the Basel market-risk framework (FRTB) sets trading-book capital requirements.
concept.intuition: It is the risk that the market itself moves against you: the everyday exposure of any open position to prices, rates, and spreads.
concept.mechanics: Measured with sensitivities (delta, vega, basis-point value), VaR, and expected shortfall; capitalized under the Basel standardized or internal-models approaches, which in the revised framework use expected shortfall models, a defined trading-book/banking-book boundary, and separate charges for non-modellable risk factors.
concept.formula: Regulatory framing: capital is a function of expected shortfall at the 97.5% level over stressed horizons plus non-modellable risk factor charges; practically, P/L approximates sum_i (sensitivity_i * factor move_i).
concept.failure_modes: Market-risk models assume continuity and measurable distributions; jumps, gaps, and correlation breakdowns violate both. Capital frameworks lag product innovation, and measures calibrated on quiet data underestimate stress-period co-movement.
concept.misconceptions: Market risk is not just 'the market going down' for a long-only book: short, hedged, and option books carry market risk in both directions and in second-order quantities (volatility, correlation, basis) that price level alone misses.
concept.example: A trading desk holding equity index futures loses in proportion to its delta on a 3% index drop; under the revised Basel framework its internal-models capital is set from expected shortfall at the trading-desk level.

citations.source: BCBS: Minimum capital requirements for market risk (revised standard)
